The wisdom of crowds, internalized. And it opens up new ways to think about how to structure and design these internal society simulations.

The social organization of thought isn't correlated with better reasoning—it's driving it. This suggests that robust reasoning, whether in humans or AI, emerges from the simulation of collective discourse.

More strikingly, the simulated personas within these debates exhibit very different personalities and background expertise. And when we train models with reinforcement learning rewarded only for accuracy, they spontaneously evolve these conversational patterns.

This mirrors how human collective intelligence works: diverse perspectives in structured dialogue outperform any single viewpoint. It provides a silicon justification for critical historical arguments about the rise of reason, per Mercier and Sperber’s book The Enigma of Reason.

Through mechanistic interpretability and large-scale analysis, we show that reasoning models spontaneously develop conversational behaviors—questioning themselves, shifting perspectives, engaging in conflict, and reconciling opposing views.
These models don't just "think longer." They generate internal multi-agent debates we call "societies of thought."

11/11 Too many of us haven’t understood yet that we’re interdependent. We’re all in it together – human, animal, plant, and machine alike.

Read the full piece: https://t.co/0rwfVScjYt
10/11 If there is any threat to our social order here, it comes not from robots but from inequalities among human beings.
9/11 AI models can embody considerable intelligence, just as human brains can, but they aren’t fellow apes vying for status. They depend on us; we may come to depend on them just as deeply.
8/11 Put simply, because we’re worried about who will be on top.

7/11 The increasing depth and breadth of collective intelligence is a good thing if we want to flourish at planetary scale, but that growth isn’t often perceived as something cumulative and mutual. Why?
6/11 What we think of as “human intelligence” is a collective phenomenon arising from cooperation among many individually narrower intelligences, like you and me.
5/11 And it has become clear that, no matter how it is embodied, intelligence requires scale. Bigger brains allow larger groups to cooperate effectively. Larger groups are, in turn, more intelligent.

4/11 However, the larger story of evolution is one in which cooperation allows simpler entities to join forces, creating larger, more complex, and more enduring ones…Mutualism is what has allowed us to scale.
3/11 We’re in the untenable position of regarding the machine as alien because we are already in the untenable position of alienating each other.
2/11 Labor is not a zero-sum game, and robots aren’t an “other” that competes with us. They’re part of humanity – and we’re partly machine.

15/15 Neither should they remain bulleted lists of desiderata posted on the web pages of standards bodies, governments, or corporations, with no direct connection to running code. They should, instead, become the legible and auditable “operating handbooks” of tomorrow’s AIs.
14/15 My view is that AI values needn’t be— and shouldn’t be— dictated by engineers, ethicists, lawyers, or any other narrow constituency.

13/15 We have early evidence that this approach works, and as language-enabled models improve generally, so too will their ability to behave according to ethical principles. This is the main point I hope to convey in this paper.

12/15 For an AI model to behave according to a given set of values, it has to be able to understand what those values are just as we would— via language. By sharing language with AIs, we can share norms and values with them too.

11/15 This is because, although our biology endows us with certain pre-linguistic moral sentiments (such as care for offspring and in-group altruism), *language* generalizes these sentiments into ethical values, whether widely held or aspirational.

10/15 Although anthropomorphism does pose its own risks, this familiarity is good news, in that it may make human value alignment more straightforward than the existential risk community has imagined.

9/15 The result isn’t an alien with inscrutable goals. Anyone can chat with a language model, and it can respond in ways so familiar that concern has shifted from worrying about AI’s alienness to worrying about our tendency to anthropomorphize it. It’s all *too* human-like!

8/15 Such doomsday scenarios were more credible in 2014, but they’re less so now that we’re starting to understand the landscape better. Language modeling has proven to be the key to making the general-purpose AI technology of the 2020s.

7/15 If AIs are highly capable but malicious, or just clueless about right and wrong, then the worst outcomes could even resemble those popularized by the very different community of philosophers and researchers who have written about AI existential risk. @DebateThoughts

6/15 Today’s AI models can engineer drugs (or poisons), design proteins, write code, solve puzzles, model people’s states of mind, control robots in human environments, and plan strategies. Whether for good or for ill, these things are hard to dismiss as mere babble.

5/15 On the other hand, if, as I argue in this paper, language models *can* understand concepts, then they’ll have far greater utility— though with this utility, we must also consider a wider landscape of potential harms and risks. Big social and policy questions arise too.

4/15 Seemingly, the best we can do is to carefully curate training inputs to filter out “toxic content”, even as we seek to broaden data sources to better represent human diversity. There are some profound challenges implied by this approach.

3/15 If, as some researchers contend, language models are mere “babblers” that randomly regurgitate their training data— “garbage in, garbage out”— then real AI value alignment is, at least for now, out of reach.
2/15 Today, this turns on the even more fundamental question of whether the newest generation of language models can or can’t understand concepts— and on what it means to understand.

1/15 Beyond the current news cycle about whether AIs are sentient is a more practical and immediately consequential conversation about AI value alignment: whether and how AIs can be imbued with human values.
